pattern.crimePattern: co-wife left with nothing kills the widow who inherited the paddies and stages a hippo attack
pattern.notes: Fictional tenants, paddy numbers and scheme staff. The co-wife relationship is written with sadness, not as a joke or a cultural judgement; the scheme clerk names the rule that left one widow with everything. Scheme tenancy procedure is for the cultural reader to confirm.

ob.text: A bird-scarer at the Ahero irrigation scheme reports a woman, Jacinta Oketch (46), found face down in an irrigation canal at 07:50. Villagers gathering on the bund say a hippo got her.

facts.text: Jacinta Oketch was found face down in an irrigation canal at Ahero at 07:50. Villagers say a hippo got her.
She was found face down in the canal below her paddy, mud on her shoulders.
Mzee Oyugi: he started scaring at 06:15 on the next bund. He saw Jacinta walk to her inlet "just after six" with her jembe. He heard nothing. At 07:50 he saw her in the water.
Mzee Oyugi was on his bird-scaring platform from 06:15, in view of two other bird-scarers.
Her inlet gate is a square-edged wooden board, opened about halfway. Her own jembe lies on the bund beside it, intact.
The "hippo trail" is a wide flattened strip into the canal, with no footprints of any kind and no rice eaten.
Mzee Oyugi: "A hippo leaves round prints the size of a plate, four toes, and it eats the rice. This is a drag mark. There's no footprint at all."
A heavy log with fresh black clay caked on its underside lies where the trail begins.
In the reeds 40 m upstream: a jembe handle, freshly snapped at the socket end, as if it broke on a heavy blow.
The canal bank below paddy 114 is black cotton clay.
Tenancy register: paddies 114–116 transferred to Jacinta Oketch on the late husband's nomination. Violet Makokha's request to split them was refused: "only the tenant can request".
Tenancy register: an objection by Silas Oketch to the transfer, dismissed.
Water committee minutes: Jacinta's complaint that the bailiff sold water turns is due to be heard in January. He was warned in writing on 1 December.
The minutes record no water dispute of any kind between the tenants of paddies 114–116.
A flyer on the scheme noticeboard: "Get a title deed for your scheme plot! Mvua Holdings. Till 880 214." Scheme land is public land; it can't be titled.
Clement: Violet came to the office twice to plead for a split. The second time she said, "Then I'll have to wait for her to go."
Clement was at home in Ahero town until he caught the 07:30 matatu to the scheme; the office opens at 08:00. The conductor knows him.
Clement: "The rules give the paddies to the nominated wife. One widow gets everything, the other gets permission. I wrote it down because it's the rule."
Clement: Violet works Jacinta's paddies for a third of the harvest. There are no debts or loans between them on the scheme's books.
Pamela: she saw Violet arrive home at about 06:40, wet to the waist, and wash at the tap.
Kevin: Silas was at the early-morning rice auction at Ahero market from 05:30 to 08:00, bidding loudly.
Sluice log: Nahashon opened the main sluice at block C, 3 km away, from 05:45 to 07:00, witnessed by two tenants.
In Violet's house: a wrap skirt, washed but still damp, with mud in the hem stitching.
Hidden in Violet's granary, wrapped in a cloth: a jembe blade with no handle, splintered wood still jammed in the socket.
Autopsy: drowning. First, a blow to the back of the head from a long rounded wooden object. Bruises on both shoulders from being held down.
Autopsy: no bite or crush injuries of any kind.
Autopsy: death between 05:30 and 07:30.
Autopsy: a healthy heart.
Comparison: the snapped end of the handle from the reeds fits the splintered wood in the socket of the blade from Violet's granary.
Lab: the mud in the skirt's hem is the black cotton clay of the canal bank below paddy 114.
Violet: "I didn't leave the house until eight. I heard the news from the neighbours."
Violet: "We were sisters. Ask anyone."
Violet admits she was at the canal below the paddies at dawn, "to wash".
Silas: "I was at the rice auction."
Silas: "My brother's land should be with the family. A woman can't hold three paddies." An ugly view; not a crime.
Nahashon: "I was opening the main sluice at block C."
Nahashon: "Yes, she reported me. I've already been warned. I'll lose my job, not my mind."

timeOfDeath.note: Alive at her inlet just after 06:00; Violet home wet at 06:40. The autopsy allows 05:30–07:30.

proof.concludes: There was no hippo: no footprints, no eaten rice, no bite or crush injuries. Jacinta was struck from behind and held under, and the trail was made by dragging a log.
All three paddies went to Jacinta on the nomination. Violet was refused a split and told the clerk she'd "have to wait for her to go".
Jacinta reached her inlet just after six. Violet didn't stay home until eight: she was at the canal at dawn and came home at 06:40, wet to the waist. Jacinta died between 06:00 and 06:40.

The snapped handle in the reeds fits the blade hidden in Violet's granary, and her skirt carries the canal-bank clay. Violet Makokha struck Jacinta with a jembe handle and held her under the water, then staged a hippo attack, because the paddies had gone to Jacinta and left her with nothing.

eliminations.why: Silas was at the rice auction from 05:30 to 08:00.
Nahashon was opening the main sluice at block C, 3 km away, from 05:45 to 07:00, with two witnesses.
Mzee Oyugi was on his bird-scaring platform from 06:15 in view of two others.
Clement was at home in Ahero town until the 07:30 matatu.
No bite or crush injuries, no prints, no rice eaten.
A blow came first, and she was held down by the shoulders.
The gate is a square-edged board; the wound is from a long rounded object.
A healthy heart; she drowned after a blow.
That grievance is Nahashon's, and he was at block C.
That claim is Silas's, already dismissed, and he was at the auction.
No water dispute was ever recorded between the co-wives.
No debts or loans: Violet worked the paddies for a share.

reconstruction.text: Last year their husband dies. On his written nomination the scheme transfers all three paddies to Jacinta, the first wife. Violet may work them "if she behaves".
Violet asks the clerk to split the tenancy. Only the tenant can ask. The second time, she says she'll have to wait for Jacinta to go.
Tuesday, just after 06:00. Jacinta walks to her inlet with her jembe. Violet follows along the bund with her own.
At the inlet Violet strikes her from behind so hard the handle snaps at the socket, and holds her under the brown water.

She throws the handle into the reeds, drags a log through the soft bank to make a trail, and takes the blade home. At 06:40 Pamela sees her washing at the tap, wet to the waist. By eight the village is saying kiboko.
